title: Practice online
hook: a man hurls insults at the Buddha, who asks whose food it is when guests refuse it: right speech in the comment section
tomorrow: why did a rich tax collector climb a tree to see Jesus?

segments.voice: This week's lines come back in the games: the poor, the common home, no hatred, neighbors, you were strangers, all creatures. Yesterday's was all creatures, from Francis's birds to every being in the Metta Sutta. Today, a loud place: the comments.
screen: `SIX LINES COME BACK.` → `ALL CREATURES.` → `NOW, THE COMMENTS.`

segments.voice: A post, a reply, a reply to the reply, and ten comments later strangers are calling each other names. The Pali texts have a man like that. Akkosaka Bharadvaja hears that a man of his clan has become a monk under the Buddha. He's furious. He goes straight to the Buddha and lets him have it: insult after insult, rude and harsh. The Buddha waits until he's finished. Then he asks him a question about guests.
screen: `TEN COMMENTS LATER.` → `A MAN ARRIVES FURIOUS.` → `INSULT AFTER INSULT.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT GUESTS.`

segments.voice: Do friends and relatives ever visit you? Sometimes, the man says. Do you offer them food? Sometimes. And if they don't accept it, whose is it? Then it's mine. In the same way, the Buddha says, I don't accept your abuse. It's all yours. The sutta ends with the man going forth as a monk himself. Under the story sits the Buddhist teaching of right speech, one part of the Noble Eightfold Path: refraining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech and idle chatter. Notice it runs both ways. Right speech is what you don't send. And the Buddha's reply shows what you don't have to take. Online, that's most of the practice. Before you post: is it true, does it divide, is it harsh, is it worth saying? And when a hostile reply lands, the food can stay on the table.
screen: `WHOSE IS THE REFUSED FOOD?` · `I DON'T ACCEPT YOUR ABUSE.` · `RIGHT SPEECH: FOUR THINGS NOT SENT.` · `THE FOOD STAYS ON THE TABLE.` · then, large: `RIGHT SPEECH ONLINE.`

segments.voice: Open a message or a comment you've meant to write, and draft one kind line. Run it past the four: true, not dividing, not harsh, worth saying. Then set the phone face down and breathe with the draft unsent until the sit is done.
Practice online: right speech in the comments. Nothing false, divisive, harsh or idle sent, and insults left unaccepted, like refused food.
Your line: right speech online. The Buddha left the insult with the one who brought it. That's the week, day 1729.

screen: `DAY 1729 COUNTS.` → `IN THE WORLD · 9 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID A RICH TAX COLLECTOR CLIMB A TREE TO SEE JESUS?`

howItsDone: Buddhists learn right speech as part of the Noble Eightfold Path, and those who take the five precepts keep one against false speech. Teachers tell the story of the refused gift of abuse to show that insults need not be taken up.

fork.setup: someone quote-posts you with a mean, half-true jab, and your friends are watching to see what you'll do. which fits right speech?
options: correct the false part once, calmly, and leave the jab alone
never post again, since anything online is idle chatter
match their tone so nobody thinks you're weak
fork.reveal: right speech still says what's true. it refuses harsh and divisive words, and the Buddha's reply shows the insult can stay with its sender.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3, shape review. The week's six lines return in games.recall; the day's word is taught lightly through a real story: the Akkosa Sutta (SN 7.2), where the Buddha leaves the abuse with the one who brought it. Teaching named: right speech in the Eightfold Path (SN 45.8). The Abhaya Sutta (used on day 1433) is avoided. Hook answers day 1728's question.

Check: in SN 7.2, Akkosaka is angered that a Bharadvaja brahmin went forth under the Buddha; after the reply he goes for refuge, is ordained and attains the goal. 'Is it true, does it divide, is it harsh, is it worth saying' is the lesson's restatement of the four abstentions, not a quotation. The precept against false speech is the fourth of the five.
